**Covalent Bond in Hydrogen:** The electronic configuration of hydrogen is $	ext{H(1)} ightarrow 1	ext{s}^1$. When $2	ext{ H}$ atoms come close, both of them share one electron from their outermost energy level each. That means, they create a pair of electrons which makes the configuration same as inert gases. This creates a $	ext{(H-H)}$ covalent bond.

$$	ext{H} oldsymbol{\cdot} +  oldsymbol{\cdot}	ext{H} ightarrow 	ext{H} oldsymbol{\cdot} oldsymbol{\cdot}	ext{H}$$

**Covalent Bond in $	ext{O}_2$ Molecule:** The electronic configuration of oxygen is $	ext{O(8)} ightarrow 1	ext{s}^2 2	ext{s}^2 2	ext{p}^4$. It lacks two electrons in its outermost energy level than that of inert gas. When two $	ext{O}$ atoms come close, both of them share two electrons from their outermost energy level each. That means, they create two pairs of electrons which makes the configuration same as inert gases. This creates a $	ext{(O=O)}$ covalent bond. Here the number of bond is two.

Generally,
$$	ext{O} + 	ext{O} ightarrow 	ext{O} = 	ext{O} \text{ or } \text{O}_2$$
